title: Section 6.0 Creating Tags and Event Types

source.author: Written for this study guide
source.grounding: help.splunk.com Splunk Enterprise 10.4, Knowledge Management Manual

questions.stem: What does a tag attach to?

options.text: A field-value pair, such as `host=web01`
options.explanation: Tags are applied to a specific value of a specific field. An event picks the tag up only because it carries that pair.

options.text: An event
options.explanation: Events acquire tags indirectly. Nothing is attached to the event itself.

options.text: A field, regardless of its value
options.explanation: Tagging a whole field would apply the label to every value it holds. Tags are value-specific.

options.text: A source type
options.explanation: You can tag `sourcetype=secure`, but that is still a field-value pair rather than the source type as an object.

questions.overallExplanation: A tag always names a pair. `host=web01`, `sourcetype=secure`, `status=404` and `eventtype=failed_login` are all taggable. This is why tagging is the standard remedy when a host value changes: the old and new values can carry the same tag.

guide.verdictNote: Tagging never changes the underlying value. It adds a searchable alternate label alongside it.

docs.title: Tag field-value pairs in search (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: Tags are assigned to field-value pairs.

questions.stem: Which search finds events where the tag `webserver` is applied specifically to the `host` field?

options.text: `tag::host=webserver`
options.explanation: The field-scoped form uses exactly two colons between tag and the field name, with no spaces.

options.text: `tag:host=webserver`
options.explanation: One colon is not the documented syntax. It is the single most common way to get this wrong.

options.text: `tags::host=webserver`
options.explanation: The pseudo-field is singular. There is no tags field.

options.text: `tag.host=webserver`
options.explanation: A dot is not a valid separator here. Splunk would read this as a field literally named tag.host.

questions.overallExplanation: Two forms exist. `tag=<tagname>` searches every tagged field-value pair regardless of field, and `tag::<field>=<tagname>` scopes the search to one field. Both accept the wildcard.

guide.verdictNote: The unscoped form is `tag=` and not `tags=`. A question in the transcribed practice bank keys `tags=` as correct, which the documentation contradicts.

docs.title: Tag field-value pairs in search (Knowledge Management 10.4)

questions.stem: Which of the following disqualifies a search string from being saved as an event type?

options.text: It contains a pipe operator after the initial search.
options.explanation: The documentation forbids an event type definition that includes a pipe after a simple search, and position in the string does not rescue it.

options.text: It contains more than one field-value pair.
options.explanation: Multiple field-value pairs joined with Boolean operators are perfectly normal in an event type.

options.text: It uses a wildcard in a field value.
options.explanation: Wildcards are allowed. `sourcetype=access_combined_wcookie` style patterns are common.

options.text: It specifies an index.
options.explanation: Naming an index is allowed and often sensible for scoping.

questions.overallExplanation: The same restriction list forbids a subsearch and forbids referencing a report with the savedsearch command. An event type is a classification rule, so it has to be a plain search expression rather than a pipeline.

guide.verdictNote: Three restrictions to carry in: no pipe, no subsearch, no savedsearch reference.

docs.title: Define event types in Splunk Web (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: An event type search cannot include a pipe operator or a subsearch.

questions.stem: Event type priorities range from 1 to 10. Which value is the highest priority?

options.explanation: The documentation states plainly that 1 is the best priority and 10 is the worst. Lower number wins.
This is the intuitive reading if you think of priority as a score, and it is the reverse of the documented scale.
Zero is outside the documented range, which starts at 1.

options.text: 5, as the midpoint and default
options.explanation: A midpoint is not a priority ranking, and priority is optional rather than defaulting to the middle.

questions.overallExplanation: Priority does two things: event types with a priority sort above those without and order among themselves by value, and only one event type colour displays per event, so the highest priority decides the colour.

guide.blueprintTitle: Describe event types and their uses
guide.verdictNote: The documentation's own example gives critical_disk_error priority 3 and a broad catch-all a worse number, which is a useful memory hook for the direction of the scale.

docs.title: About event type priorities (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: Priority is 1 through 10, where 1 is best and 10 is worst.

questions.stem: An event matches three different event types. What does the `eventtype` field contain?

options.text: All three names, as a multivalue field.
options.explanation: A single event can match many event types, and eventtype behaves as a multivalue field when it does.

options.text: Only the highest-priority name.
options.explanation: Priority orders the values and decides the displayed colour, but it does not discard the others.

options.text: Only the first name alphabetically.
options.explanation: Alphabetical order plays no part in selecting a single winner, because there is no single winner.

options.text: The three names concatenated into one string.
options.explanation: They are separate values in a multivalue field, not a joined string.

questions.overallExplanation: eventtype is multivalue when several event types match. The values are ordered by priority score first, then alphabetically, and only one colour displays per event.

guide.blueprintTitle: Describe event types and their uses
guide.verdictNote: Because eventtype is a field like any other, it can itself be tagged, which is how `eventtype=failed_login` ends up carrying a CIM tag such as authentication.

docs.title: About event types (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: An event can match multiple event types; eventtype is multivalue in that case.

questions.stem: How does an event type differ from a report?

options.text: An event type classifies matching events automatically at search time; a report is a saved search you run to get a result set.
options.explanation: One is a passive classification applied to data, the other is an action that produces results on demand or on a schedule.

options.text: They are the same object under two names in the UI.
options.explanation: They are separate knowledge objects with separate management pages and separate conf files.

options.text: An event type can be scheduled; a report cannot.
options.explanation: Scheduling belongs to reports and alerts. An event type has no schedule.

options.text: A report classifies events; an event type returns a result set.
options.explanation: The two roles are swapped here.

questions.overallExplanation: An event type is a category that attaches itself to every matching event whenever a search runs. A report is a stored search that you execute. This is also why an event type definition cannot reference a report with savedsearch.

guide.blueprintTitle: Describe event types and their uses
guide.verdictNote: Reports are not on the SPLK-1002 blueprint in their own right. They appear here only as the thing an event type is contrasted with.

docs.title: About event types (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: Event types categorise events at search time, unlike saved searches.

questions.stem: In the sequence of search-time operations, which comes last?

options.text: Tags
options.explanation: Tags are the ninth and final step, which is why a tag can be applied to an event type but an event type cannot be built on a tag.

options.text: Event types
options.explanation: Event types are step eight, immediately before tags.

options.text: Lookups
options.explanation: Lookups are step seven, before both event types and tags.

options.text: Calculated fields
options.explanation: Calculated fields are step six, before lookups.

questions.overallExplanation: The nine steps in order: field filters, EXTRACT-, REPORT-, KV_MODE, FIELDALIAS-, EVAL-, LOOKUP-, event types, tags. Most cross-section questions on this exam resolve to a position in this list.

guide.verdictNote: Nine operations, not the six taught in most courses. The extra three are the distinct extraction mechanisms EXTRACT-, REPORT- and KV_MODE.

docs.title: The sequence of search-time operations (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: Tags are the final search-time operation.

questions.stem: Which statement about priority and colour is correct?

options.text: They are properties of an event type, and an event type can itself be tagged.
options.explanation: Priority and colour belong to the event type object. Because eventtype is a field, `eventtype=<name>` can then be tagged like any other pair.

options.text: They are properties of a tag.
options.explanation: Tags have neither. They are a name attached to a field-value pair and carry no display attributes.

options.text: They are properties of both tags and event types.
options.explanation: Only event types have them.

options.text: Colour belongs to the event type and priority belongs to the tag.
options.explanation: Both belong to the event type. Splitting them between the two objects is a distractor pattern.

questions.overallExplanation: Priority and colour are event type attributes. A statement pairing tags with priority or colour is wrong, but a statement saying you can tag an event type that has a priority and a colour is correct, which is a distinction worth reading carefully in exam wording.

guide.blueprintTitle: Describe event types and their uses
guide.verdictNote: The printed Apress guide keys a question on this incorrectly, which is recorded in source-notes/apress-errata.md.

docs.title: About event type priorities (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: Priority and colour are configured on the event type.

questions.stem: A host was renamed for an input, so historical events carry `host=old-name` and new events carry `host=new-name`. Both must be searchable together without editing the data. What is the standard remedy?

options.text: Apply the same tag to both `host=old-name` and `host=new-name`, then search by tag.
options.explanation: Tagging adds a shared searchable label to both pairs while leaving the underlying values untouched.

options.text: Create a field alias mapping old-name to new-name.
options.explanation: Aliases map field names to other field names, not one value of a field to another value.

options.text: Reindex the historical data with the new host value.
options.explanation: Reindexing is expensive and unnecessary when a search-time label solves it.

options.text: Define a calculated field that rewrites host on the older events.
options.explanation: This would overwrite the real value, losing the information about which physical input produced the event.

questions.overallExplanation: This is the canonical use of tags: one label spanning several values of the same field. It works retroactively because tags are applied at search time, and it never mutates the stored value.

guide.verdictNote: The same shape of answer applies to normalising several source-specific values onto one CIM tag, which is where sections 6.0 and 10.0 meet.

docs.title: Tag field-value pairs in search (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: Tags let you group several field values under one searchable name.

questions.stem: Which two statements about managing tags in Splunk Web are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Settings, Tags offers views by field-value pair, by tag name, and all unique tag objects.
options.explanation: Three distinct views exist, each useful for a different task.

options.text: Disabling a tag from the List by tag name page disables it across all apps that contain it.
options.explanation: That page operates on the tag name globally rather than on one field-value pairing.

options.text: Tags are defined in eventtypes.conf using the `tags` attribute.
options.explanation: That attribute exists but the spec marks it deprecated and points to tags.conf. Tags on an event type live in tags.conf under `[eventtype=<name>]`.

options.text: A tag can only be applied to one field-value pair at a time.
options.explanation: The same tag name can be applied to many pairs, which is what makes tags useful for normalisation.

questions.overallExplanation: Three views, and a global effect when disabling by tag name. The conf file to know is tags.conf, with stanza headers of the form `[eventtype=<name>]` when tagging an event type.

guide.verdictNote: Knowing which conf file owns which object is reliably worth a mark: tags.conf for tags, eventtypes.conf for event types, props.conf for aliases and calculated fields, macros.conf for macros, workflow_actions.conf for workflow actions.
